projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with David Ferris was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran David Ellison Ferris. Mr. Ferris served in the US Army Air Corps with the Eighth Air Force, 379th Bomb Group. He served in the European theater and his highest rank was second lieutenant. And Mr. Ferris was a prisoner of war. I am Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded at Mr. Ferris' home in Mansfield, Ohio, on July 17th, 2004. David was 82 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: We were--I was living in Cleveland Heights, Ohio. And--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you? When were you--when were you born?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: I was born in 1922; so, at that time, I was 19 years old.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Out of school, working at that point?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: I had--I graduated from high school in 1939. I worked a year to make the money to go to Case School of Applied Science for one year. Found out I didn't wanna be an engineer and I signed up for the Aviation Cadets. Now that would have been in the fall of 1942, I believe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Before you got to that, do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Oh, I sure do. I was at the house of an aunt and uncle, and two cousins and, and I were up in a bedroom. And I can remember havin' the radio on, and they came on with the announcement of the bombing of Pearl Harbor. I think this was about early noon or one o'clock, maybe. And I can't say that it meant a whole lot to me right at, right at the moment. We--one cousin's the same age as I and the other was two years younger. And we were just horsin' around and Pearl Harbor didn't mean a whole lot.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. So, there wasn't a desire to run out and sign up the next day--

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --or anything like that?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No. I woulda been 19 years old, all right, at that time, but- No. Right away I didn't think about it. But then when I got to thinkin' about what was gonna happen and so forth , why, I thought I would like to be a fighter pilot. And I signed up for the Aviation Cadets. That woulda been in the fall of '42, I believe. And at that time, there was a wait of about a year before they took ya. They had plenty of volunteers for the Aviation Cadet Program. So I was finally called in January of '43. Or I mighta got the notice before that. But in January of '43, I went to Nashville, Tennessee, which was a classification center. And they told me they're gonna make a navigator out of me instead of fighter pilot. This was a big blow (emphasis given) at the time. But I'd had the math, math background and they needed navigators and anybody that had any math, I guess, that was pretty much what you were gonna be doin'. So went to--from Nashville, Tennessee, went to Selman Field in Monroe, Louisiana, for navigational training and that took from February till September, I guess. I graduated sometime around the middle of September in '43, as a second lieutenant. And then from there it was on to Pyote, Texas which was called a staging area. They put the crew together and we flew mi--practiced missions outta there. And that lasted till December, the first part of December, I guess. Then it was on to Grand Island, Nebraska. We picked out our airplane and were on our way overseas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get along with your crew--the guys in your crew?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. No problem there at all. They broke us up into two halves. One half was sent overseas by ship and the other half of us were gonna fly over with the aid of an ATC crew, an Air Transport C-Command crew. Well, we got goin' and we had engine trouble and we landed in Detroit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of plane were you flyin'?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: B-17s, okay.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah. And we landed there on a Friday afternoon and they said they wouldn't get anything done till Monday, so I took off for Cleveland. I told--they told us that we were on orders and if we left there we'd be AWOL. Well, I had in mind givin' my wife a ring and took off for Cleveland from Detroit. I got a--actually got a--hitchhiked home. Got home and ended up--on Saturday we went down and bought the ring. Hadn't had--I don't know if you want all this information.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. Yes. Definitely.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Okay. We hadn't asked her folks at all and she was only--she still hadn't finished her senior year in high school. She was in, in her junior year in high school. So we bought the ring with the idea that if her folks were against it, she would take the ring back. And so we did that and went home and asked her parents. She first asked--she first called both her sisters to come and give her moral support. And the younger sister was all for it--w-w-was ten years older than Nancy. Her older sister was 13 years older. And she thought it was not a good idea. She wasn't even allowed to date at her age. But at any rate, her folks did give her approval. So then on Sunday afternoon, I actually was able to hitch a ride from the airport back--hitch on a military plane back to Detroit. So I got back there all right. Detroit, we flew to Manchester, New Hampshire. Had more engine troubles. They worked on it there. From there we went to Bangor, Maine. Had more problems. From Bangor, Maine, we went to Gander, Newfoundland. More troubles. From there to Goose Bay, Labrador. Finally, we got to Scotland. It took us six weeks. The guys who went by ship were there a long time waiting for us. So then, sat around for a couple days, they got assigned to the bomb group, which was the three se-seventy-ninth. And that was--that was sometime in early January. Went to--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That'd be '44, right?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: '44, yeah. And from there they assigned us then to the 379th Bomb Group which was in Kimbolton, England. And it didn't take very much training. We flew our first mission on February 4th, 1944. That--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember--have specific memories of that first mission?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Oh, sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Tell me as much as you can about that.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Well, the first mission was to Frankfurt, Germany. I actually flew 12 missions. Four of 'em were to Frankfurt because that was the center of all transportation in Germany. All the railro--that was the center of Germany. All the railroad yards came into Frankfurt. So the idea was to bomb those yards to disrupt the transportation. Well, Frankfurt was heavily defended with antiaircraft fire. Once they--they decided wh-where you 're comin' from and where you're goin', they set up these big boxes of flak, which was .88 millimeter shells, bursting in little black bombs. Ya had to fly right through that into the target. Once you set yer course for the target, there was no changing. You just flew right through that flak. The only good part of that was ya didn't have any fighters on yer tail at that time because they didn't wanna fly through the flak. So on the very first mission, I saw a plane explode in the air from the flak. Got a direct hit, obviously, and exploded and didn't see any chutes or anything. So that was kind of yer "Welcome to Germany," you know, and it scared the hell out of ya. We did have some fighter problems on the way in and the way out. And as a navigator, I had a .50 caliber gun on each side of the nose. The bombardier was in the nose with a chin turret. Now, I always--we always flew in formation. I was never the lead navigator. I never did any navigation. I was a gunner. {laughter} And so the fighter attacks were not anything great on that first mission, but I did get to shoot a little bit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did ya get close to hittin' anything?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Not on that mission. There was another mission when I got partial credit for shooting down a, a plane. Could be sure--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: --exactly who got it, but- So that's really the significance of the first mission, I would say. We got back, had a few holes in the airplane, nothing much.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wh-what did you feel when you got back from that mission? Did--was there any time to think about what you had been through?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah. You know, they always took you in for debriefing and gave you a shot of whiskey. {laughter} I can just remember the relief, you know: It's nice to be on the ground again. And that was about the extent of it, probably. But I flew 12 missions altogether. That first one was on February 4th. The last one was on March 2nd. That wa--the last one was also to Frankfurt. In between, the most significant one was the one to Schweinfurt. We came back with over 400 holes in the airplane. That was all antiaircraft fire, probably, although we had fighter attack, so I can't say it was all, but- We were just very lucky to get back on that one. That was the worst mission we had, period, until the last one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any of the crew on any of those first dozen missions?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Nope. Didn't lose any crew and didn't have any significant injuries. On the last mission, I was the only one of the crew that was hit, and I had a piece of flak go through my knee. We had bombed Frankfurt and were on our way home and around Brussels we ran into heavy a-a-antiaircraft fire. And I was sitting on a case of ammunition, and this piece of flak went through my knee and hit me in the elbow. Well, it coulda just as well been a little higher and hit me in the heart, say, and--but all I knew at first was I thought I had a hit in the elbow and then blood started coming out of the bunny blue heated suit. And so then I bandaged that up. And very shortly after that we got a direct hit on the wing tanks. And the pilot gave the order to bail out. So then it was just the matter of snapping on the chest pack for the harness--for the, for the parachute. And we had a little hatch about, oh, 18 by 24 in the nose and took that off and dove out and- Actually the, the ride down in the chute--I opened up before I should of. They had always told us that should wait for the horizon to be coming up. Well, heck, {laughter} you wanna make sure that chute's gonna open, so I did pull it too soon. And I had a--I was down fairly low and a German Me109 circled me. And there had been stories that they would knock off chutists, you know. You never knew. He mighta lost a good friend or his family mighta been bombed or who knows what. But he circled me and dipped his wings and took off. So that was a big relief. Then I landed in an open field, an open plowed field, started talking the chute off and rollin' it up. And pretty soon a farmer came out and he had coveralls and wooden shoes and a tam and a pitchfork to dress me like a farmer. But he found out I'd been wounded. And he said, "We don't"--he was part of the underground--and he said, "We don't have any medical facilities. You're better off to let the Germans capture ya, and they'll take ya into a hospital. Well, so that's exactly what happened then. I started walking along a hedgerow and came to a corner and I went around that corner and ran into a German patrol. And the bandages slipped off my knee down to my ankle. And I reached down to pull that bandage up and he pulled the rifle up in my chest. He didn't know what I was reaching for, and- But anyhow, "For you the 'var' is over," is what he said. {laughter} "For you the 'var' is over." (Speaking with a German accent.) So he took me into town. The town was--it was either Mons, M-o-n-s or Athis. I landed near one and they took me into Gestapo headquarters in the other one because I was in civilians clothes. And they kept me up a good bit of the night.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So had that underground, he had given you civilian clothes? The underground guy? Or why were you in civilian clothes?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Oh, he brought me out these coveralls.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh. Oh. So he did, yeah. Okay, at that point.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: I was in coveralls, dressed like a farmer. But I had my uniform underneath.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Then that's when he realized you were wounded and couldn't help you.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. So they kept threatening to shoot me as a spy. I was in civilian clothes. Ya know, all ya tell 'em was name, rank, and serial number. And they said, well, they--I don't know if I told 'em my bomb group or not. I can't imagine that I did. But they did know I was from the 379th Bomb Group. They told me the colonel who was the commanding officer of the group. And they knew more about it than I did, you know. There was nothing that I coulda told 'em that was--woulda, woulda done them any good. But, I started passing out on them. I'd lost quite a bit of blood. So the next morning they took me into Brussels to a German Air Force hospital. And I was operated on by the head German doctor who had trained at Johns Hopkins in this country and interned in Boston. And he said he was a, a German, but not a Nazi. He said, "Someday, I hope I get back to the states." So I took his name, or I remembered his name, and I turned it in after the war. But I never had any idea of how that worked out. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they tell you to do that if you were gettin' nice treatment, or did you--

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No, I just did it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --just do that on your own?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Just did it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Just figured that out--yeah. He just__+--

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: I mean, while I was being operated on in that operating room, there was two interns operating on Germans. And he operated on me himself. So I spent seven weeks in that hospital. And I had a nurse--another story--it was--her name was Schwester Linda, Sister Linda. And she kinda took care of me. She'd bring me fresh eggs. What I had to do is put a hole in that egg and suck it out. The first time she told me what she wanted to do I said, "No way." 'Ooma sessen. Ooma sessen.' (ph) (Sie mussen essen) You know, "You must eat." So I learned to do it, and- But, like I say, I was there seven weeks and then it was on to Dulag Luft in Frankfurt, which was another questioning area. And that didn't amount to anything, really. Was only there a matter of a few days. I don't remember exactly. Then into a train and on to Stalag Luft 1, the prison camp. And that took a couple or three days. It was a slow goin' thing. And this was pretty cold weather, but- There was something else I s-started to tell ya about that experience there--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: At the Dulag would they--they really didn't interrogate you much at all then?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They did not think that you could help them, or did they__?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No. I'd been in the hospital, you know, all that time and I wasn't--I wasn't new news or anything. So I didn't get any threats or anything there. But, I was on crutches for a good while when I got to the prison camp. And my prison camp experience was nothing really eventful. Ended up--I couldn't--they did have some sports equipment. Guys could p-play soccer, but I wasn't in shape to do that. So I played bridge a lot. And when first got there, we got a Red Cross parcel every week. And that had, like, five packs of cigarettes in it, a couple of chocolate D-bars, some SPAM, corned beef and so forth. So it was a supplement to whatever the Germans gave you. And we got that for, oh, maybe, the first six months maybe. But then it started getting sporadic. And then the last three months, we didn't see any of 'em. 'Cause the Germans needed the food themselves, and so they didn't get 'em to us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you first you got the parcel, were you getting your own parcel or were you splitting them?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No, you first got your own. Yeah. Then you had to split 'em, all right, as time went on. But the cigarettes in there were the medium of exchange. We could use them to buy stuff from the guards. W-we had a radio in the room. We got BBC. They, they had kind of a newsletter that--or somebody put out some kind of a newsletter, which was a German slant on things. And their war news was much different than we got from BBC, you know. We knew exactly what was goin' on. And they had raids all the time. They knew that we were getting information. They had raids. But we had a tile stove, a yellow tile stove. And this little radio was hidden behind tiles on that stove. When the Germans would come in on a raid they yell--the call would go out, "Goons on the floor," you know. And that was the time to hide anything like the radio or anything else that ya didn't- The one memorable experience there was we had laundry jubs--we had the same clothes on all the time we were there. You know, I had the same--same shirt, pants, and everything. But we did launder, though, once in a while. We had a laundry tub. But mostly we used that laundry tub to take prunes and raisins and ferment 'em and make wine. {laughter} And the one time, "goon on the floor," there was an inspection coming. So what do you do with a whole tub of wine there? Everybody took clothes and threw it in there, you know. And when it was all over ya wring out the clothes and still drink the wine. {laughter} So that was the only thing that was kinda like Hogan's Heroes. You know, Hogan's Heroes' a prison camp that was always a lot of humor goin' on. We didn't have much. But I played bridge most all the - that was the biggest pastime. And again, cigarettes were the medium of exchange for winning or losing. I didn't smoke then, so I, I would trade them for D-bars, the chocolate bars, you know, and... So then, at the end, the Russians came through, overran the camp. They went through town and they took everything in sight. You know, they just cleaned house pretty much. But we had the better part of a week. So, anyhow, the Russians liberated us and we had to wait for transportation. We were right next to a German flak school. They, they had girls in there, training 'em for antiaircraft fire, you know. Well, these were young girls, and--primarily--and they'd parade along that fence. The fence was right along the border of our camp, and the guys would go out there and whistle and so forth. Well, the German commandant didn't like that and so he said, "No more of that. Any more of that, you will be shot." Well, all I remember is one guy--one guy did get shot. And that ended that. There was no more whistling at those girls. But along with that flak school, there was an airport there. And that was done purposely, I'm sure, because that kept that airport from bein' bombed. The prison camp was right next to it. We ended up having over 10,000 guys in the prison camp. There was probably 2,000 Englishmen there that some of them had been there since the Battle of Britain in 1939, you know, and- At, at the time of the Battle of the Bulge. there was a green division thrown into that. I believe it was 104th Infantry.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's right. Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: And the Germans overran them. When they went--when they--when they made their counterattack on the bulge. And those guys--a big number of 'em were brought into our camp. Well, they didn't have any barracks for 'em. They put 'em up in tents and there was a north compound and a south compound. And they filled up that north compound. And here this was right in December, you know, cold. And supposedly that was the coldest winter on record, so those poor guys were put up out there. But anyhow. Then we were flown--they brought B-17s into that airport and we were flown into France to Camp Lucky Strike. And the highlight of that was they put big platters of French bread on the table. And, I mean, that tasted like the best cake you could ever have, that French bread and butter. And I spent six weeks there. By the time I came home my cheeks were puffy from eatin' that bread. People said, "You didn't--you couldn't of had it so bad," you know. {laughter} But they finally had to ration that bread because guys were just--oh, there were stories that guys--I don't know if they actually died from overeating or not--but there were stories like that. But couldn't help make--makin' a pig of yourself on it anyhow. So it was--it took six weeks there to wait for transportation. Meanwhile, another fellow and I decided to take off, and we went up to Scotland. We knew we were gonna to be there a long time. So we went up to Scotland. And went up to Edinburgh and just did some sightseeing. I really wanted to get to Ireland. My parents were born in Northern Ireland, and--but we just decided we didn't have enough time to do that, so. So then it was back to Lucky Strike. And got the t-transportation finally and came home by ship. Landed at Fort Dix in New Jersey and then on home to Cleveland Heights, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where was Stalag Luft 1?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: It was on the Baltic Sea. The closest town was Barth, B-a-r-t-h. That wasn't a very big town. The closest town of any size was Rostock. Rostock. On the Baltic Sea. We have since been back there. On the 40th anniversary of the day we were liberated--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was that date?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: May 6th, I think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Of, of '45, right?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. An ex-POW was in the travel business, arranged a tour. And there was about a hundred of us altogether that went on this tour. And we were actually at the site of Stalag Luft 1 on the 40th anniversary of liberation. Well, there was nothing left there in the way of barracks or anything. There was a memorial that had been built, and there was still some buildings where the flak school and the airport had be-been. And from our room you could see a steeple of a cathedral. And so from the sight of that cant--cathedral was still there and that spire, so it give us a feel for where we were and what we saw. And we, we did Stalag Luft 1 and then we did Stalag Luft 3, which was the other big Air Force officer's camp. Luft 1 was all commissioned officers. And Luft 3 was pretty much the same. Now, that was in Poland, Sagan, S-a-g-a-n, Sagan, Poland. So we did that. And then we had a side trip down to Dresden. Dresden had been heavily bombed by the--by the British. The Br--the Germans had fire bombed Coventry, England, and the British, in retaliation, fire bombed Co--Dresden. And so we saw that. And that was still a mess. They sti--the Germans had not started to rebuild. They have since then, I guess. But that was--at that time, that was East Germany.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. __+

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: In fact, we got in there--I think the Wall came down in November something, and we were in there in May, so within six months roughly. And he arranged a dinner for a few of us at the house of a man who had been Director of Transportation for the East Germans, at least for, for the German part. Had about half a dozen of us to his house. And I don't know how I was picked out, but I was. And it was interesting. He was in a double house, and the occupant of the other house was a surgeon and his wife was a nurse. Now these were very ordinary houses, but he said that in East Germany under the Communists a surgeon was no better off than a worker. They were--they were treated the same, you know. Roughly, roughly the same pay scale and so forth. So, so that was interesting to see how those folks live. By then, he was a--I don't know what he was doin'. But anyhow, he was able to furnish us a meal and tell us a little bit about how things were goin' and so forth. So--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any other specific memories of day you were liberated?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Well, there was lots of cheering. You know, we were allowed to run free then until we got transportation, so we went over to that air base. And part of the air base they had a concentration camp much like the ones that are so famous. And down in the basement, there were bunk beds and there were--called 'em DPs, displaced persons. We had them working in the prison camp. They actually did the dirty work, cleaned the latrines and that sort of thing because we were commissioned officers. By the Geneva Convention we didn't have to do any labor. And so we had DPs workin' in the prison camp. But obviously they had 'em workin' over at this air base. Well, my golly. There were people lyin' in those bunks that were just skin and bones and there was a stench down there like you wouldn't believe. So that's the one memory of the liberation that sticks out, you know, that ya actually saw, you might say, a concentration camp or whatever. But other than that, it was just a matter of--we were in contact with our side and knew that we were going to be taken out of there. You know, just a matter of having to wait for the transportation. So we, we didn't do anything particular, really, that I recall.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The Russians did get to you first, though?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, yeah. They came through there first.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they make any attempt to take you guys--

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --back east?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not with the officers, huh?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No. No, not at all. They were interested in goin' after the Germans.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: ?But still__+?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: They just kept right on movin' towards the west all right. And like I say, they pillaged and ransacked everything they could. That's the story we kept getting anyhow, and- But, we saw very little of the Russians. In fact, you know, they came through there, some of 'em in horses and wagons. They had Studebaker trucks. They didn't--we didn't see any tanks or any, any real heavy combat equipment. All I remember was they were pullin' stuff with horses and wagons_ even, you know. They were quite primitive compared to what we were used to. But they sure didn't bother us in any way-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now you were, I guess, you were probably in that camp when D-Day happened, right?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah, we were.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you remember hearing that news__?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reaction when you heard that?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Well, I can remember one letter that I sent home sayin' I thought we'd be out of there by Christmas. {laughter} It proved to be wrong, but-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did that letter get through okay without any censoring?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah, it did. All I said was, "I hope to see you by Christmas." They let that go through all right. But, you know, you didn't write anything much in those letters, though. And they were very short. My wife still says she didn't get very many of 'em. {laughter}

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {laughter} Did you not write a lot, or did you not__+?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: You didn't write a lot. You know, you were board to death. There wasn't much to write about.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: All they wanted--they just wanted to hear that you were alive. It took three months to know that I was alive. They got the missing in action, and that was in March. They didn't know till June sometime that I was actually alive and a POW. So-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get much mail from your wife?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That got through okay, to you?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: They would come, maybe, six or eight at a time, you know. They came through, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the reaction when ya started hearing about what was happening with the Battle of the Bulge? Did that seem bleak?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: You know, I don't remember the specifics of that. You know, as far as how far did the Germans go through our lines and so forth. Didn't know that really till later. But then I knew--we knew that they beat 'em back again, and so--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So they might no have been reporting--on the Allied radio they might not have been reporting how bad it was, actually. {slight laughter}

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Maybe not.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And that's what you were listening to, yeah.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. Maybe not.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How about when they, they heard about the, the death of FDR?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: I don't specifically remember that either.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Don't specifically remember about that, yeah.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Nope.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any others--things you remember about the life in a prison camp?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No. They--you know, they didn't really maltreat us. At the end there, food was very short. We would get a small ration of potatoes. Once in a while, you'd get some horse meat, some turnips. But it was kind of a subsistence thing. They sure didn't have any extra food. So that, that made things worse. That winter has been--the winter that we were there, supposedly, was one of the worst in history as far as cold is concerned. We did get some cold--we were in a barracks of 24 men. All double-decker bunks, and ya had a straw mattress, slept in your clothes all the time. Always were cold in that winter.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have a particularly close buddy in that camp?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah, a fellow by the name of Gene McCready. He and I were the two that took off for Scotland. He was--we got married in August of '45, and he was in our wedding. But then he, he moved to California and never did see 'im again. We corresponded for a while. And he actually died pretty young, and so lost track of him. And the guys in the room, there were one or two--when we were--when we came back here--that was May of '45--had like a leave until the latter part of August. We actually got married on August--17th or 16th--17th. There's three days in a row, the 16th, 17th, and 18th: my mother's birthday, our wedding, and our first daughter. At any rate, only had a short time after the wedding till I had to report to Miami Beach for what they call "rehabilitation." And spent two months down there and was finally released in October. But went to the hospital every day down there. We stayed on Miami Beach in a beachfront hotel. And cost us a buck and a half a day. And every night you could go to the hotel next-door and pick out your steak and they'd cook it the way you wanted it and- That hotel we stayed in was called the Hotel Good. It was later torn down and became the Fonted Blue Hotel, which was a big--became a big fancy place. And the one next-door was the Lord Tarleton where we would go to eat, had all our meals out. And finally, we got tired of eating out and I knew I was going to be there awhile and darned if we didn't go and rent an apartment. Got--so we could have somethin' of our own. And did that until the time was up. So, I don't know, sometime the middle of October was finally released. So--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Workin' backward a little bit: Do you have specific memories of the day that you actually saw your wife when you got back to the States, that reunion?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Ye--well, it was funny. I got into Cleveland Heights and my mother wasn't home. I went there. She was at the beauty parlor. And she--it took her a long time to get over there, but she wasn't even home when I got home. And then I called Nancy's place and we got together and some partyin' went on all right. And what--you know, I don't remember specifically, really. It all kinda went together there, but-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Kinda workin' backwards a little bit to fill in some detail: When you made that parachute jump, was that your first jump, actual jump?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: One and only all right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's what I've heard from other guys that went through what you went through, that you were instructed on what to do, but you didn't actually make a jump--

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --until the order came__+.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No. That's right. You had that chest pack. There was two snaps here. Put that on. And you knew where the rip cord was. And, like I say, they--we were at 21,000 feet; so, you know, your oxygen is pretty scarce there--up there, and that's one reason they told ya not to open the chute right away. So I didn't open it right away, but I wasn't down as far as they told you, you should wait to, to go. You know, I, I got this Mighty Eighth War Diary. Have you seen this before?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I probably have, and I certainly know of--about the author. I've seen him on television--

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --and talked to another guy that talked to him actually.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Okay. Well every, every mission that I was on--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --is in there?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: --is in here, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any good luck charms or anything on your missions?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No. No. There's a picture of our crew.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right. Great. Was this the name of the plane you flew the whole time?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No. No. That was just staged. That picture was just staged.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did your--the plane you were--did you fly one particular plane, or were you in __different planes?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No, we didn't. We didn't.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. So you didn't have any particular nose art or anything on the planes you were on, huh?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No. There's been a couple articles written in the paper, the Mansfield Paper, about things, but- There's another picture. Oh, that--this--oh, this is actually in the book. This is a picture of our crew coming off of a mission.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: And that's me there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. That's great.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Tells you somethin' down there about it, but-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that was Carol Dawn, huh?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: That plane was. Now, I don't know that, that there was any significance to us on that plane. You'd be on one plane and get shot up pretty bad, and the next day you'd be on somethin' else, ya know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So did he--this book is--has information about all the missions of the Mighty Eighth?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow. That's great.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I didn't realize that __+.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Exactly. Right from the beginning. It's a history of 'em, the Eighth Air Force.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Ever been to that museum in Savannah for the Mighty Eighth?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No. I've been to Savannah because I was in the paper business. There's a big paper mill there I did business with, but I never got to the--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It seems nice. It just opened up a few years ago.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Ah. No. There's a--there's also a POW Museum--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I've been there.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: --in Anderson--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I've--I've donated to that.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: --South Carolina.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: My dad was a POW. I don't usually mention it.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Was he?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Exactly. Yeah. In the infantry though.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He got a little bit different treatment.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah. Exactly. Exactly.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Those guys had to do la--hard labor all right. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you--I, I don't know--I don't think I asked you this--did you get along okay with the guards in your camp?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah. The guards were all old men, you might say. They weren't--they weren't cannon fodder for the front, I guess you could--whatever, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: They wanted younger guys to be in the infantry and so forth. So they were old men__ for some. Like I said, they put a radio together. I don't remember too--I was never involved in any of that. I was not on an escape committee. You know, they did have such things. There was escapes attempted from the camp. But I was--I was not involved in any of that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any successful escapes from the camp?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No. No. There were guys that got outside, but they never--they never got anyplace. We were in kind of a remote area, wooded. On, on the one side, I mean. The one side was that airbase and flak school, but-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there any retaliation against the other people in the camp after there was an escape attempt?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: The only retaliation was the guys they caught trying to escape. Supposedly, they got soltar-solitary confinement for awhile, you know. But, I never even had any contact. Never talked to anybody that was in on an escape. Never really heard directly from anybody. We were- You know there's a website for our prison camp?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I'm, I'm, I'm, sure of that 'cause I've seen there are websites all over the place for all the camps--

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --I think. Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: We were in the first barracks as you come into the camp. The camp headquarters were right across the road from us, and- We were not off by ourselves, I mean, where you'd be- And I didn't get out and circulate a whole lot, talkin' to other guys, you know. So I wasn't privy to plans and so forth for escapes or anything else and- All I can re-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When they--when they got the news off the radio, did they spread that around to the guys verbally or did they-

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They didn't wr--try to write anything out because--

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Oh, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --that would be too risky.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No. See, that was in our own room. We would talk to other guys in the barracks, maybe. But, I didn't ge--even get involved in that stuff. So-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Workin' backwards: Do you--what do you remember about life in England before you were shot down?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Well, we got weekend pass--see, I was only there two months.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: We got weekend passes. And one time we invited to a family for dinner and--I don't remember if that was at Christmas or not right now. Christmas didn't amount to much. I mean as far as bein'--but I can--yeah, we invited to a family's house for--and then I remember staying at a hotel in London and Clark Gable was supposedly there. Didn't see 'im. It was that famous, famous hotel right on Piccadilly Circus, Royal--oh well, it doesn't matter. But you'd get the pass to go into London, you know, go to the Red Cross Club and dance and drink {laughter} and- So you look forward to those times. But I wasn't there long enough to enjoy a whole lot of it, you know. So over all, I just feel I'm awful damn lucky to be here. I could have been knocked off in the airplane. I could have been knocked off by the Gestapo on the ground. I got good treatment in that hospital. Here I am, 82 years old. We're talkin' about almost--well, 60 years ago that I was in that camp all right. In fact, March 2nd of this year it was 60 years ago that I was shot down. So here I am in pretty good shape for that age, and-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You sure are. END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Can't look back on that too many--made a fighter pilot out of me. I moved pretty quick and I made it back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: You know?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But when you got over there, there was still plenty of fighter opposition, wasn't there? When you started--

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Oh, heavy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --flying. Yeah. In the spring of '45?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Heavy. Heavy. There's what I looked like in the prison camp. {laughter}

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh. They took these pictures of all the prisoners?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: I guess so. And then, you know, when we went through the offices after the Russians came through, we were able to get this stuff.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, if any--I will read this for the microphone. Your prison number looks like it's 4521. That was the--your number as a prisoner?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Exactly

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Second Lieutenant, Ferris DE. What's DE?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: David Ellison.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Oh, oh. Your name. For your name

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: David Ellison

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And then this German abbreviation: ?kriegsge...,? (ph) whatever. That must be the abbreviation for__+

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Well, kriegsgefangen. KGF is kriegsgefangen.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Kriegsgefangen.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: That means prisoner of war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: LG.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: And I don't know what the rest of that is.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But that one at the end might be- Well, that's interesting. I know--I still haven't been able to figure out if they did this with the infantry. I've seen other pictures from airborne prisoners. I've seen one of those, too. Are you a member of the Barbed Wire Buckeyes? The--

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Well, I--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --American ex-POW's?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: I, I attended a couple of meetings, but they meet over in Wooster, Ohio. And, I don't know. I just--I just never was too inclined to-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. My dad paid his dues, but never went to the meetings. Never met any of the guys, but he did--he paid the dues so he could get__+.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: There's a book I started in the prince camp.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow! Is this a little bit of a diary?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yes. Yeah, a little bit. And it lists the missions we did. And these are the other members of the crew.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did the guards--did they know you were keeping this and they didn't care, or-

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Oh, I'm sure they did. They probably gave us the book. Somebody along the way gave us that book.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It says on the front here "A damn prisoner."

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah, right. Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (reading from diary) "Shot down March 2nd, 1944. Plane hit by flak over Brussels. I landed near Athus in Belgium, Belgium. Bailed out at 20,000 feet. Wound by flak in right knee. __+ No other crew member wounded. Landed in open plowed field. Arrived at the Dulag on April 17th. Left for Stalag Luft 1 on April 19th." And it looks like you arrived there April 22nd, 1944.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Never any word of anybody in the crew. So you never heard about the rest of the guys?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And they were taken--the officers were taken--

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Well, five of them got home through the Underground.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, they did?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, wow.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Which would have happened with me if I hadn't been wounded.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: The pilot took about three months to get to London through the Underground. Ya know, they worked ya thr--we were in Belgium, went through France, Spain and then to England and then home. And so five of 'em got home that way. I never ran into any of 'em until--mmm, one year the 379th Bomb Group had a reu--I mean--the POW's had a national meeting in Cleveland. And the 379th Bomb Group had, like, a table there where you registered and so forth. And I was standing there and somebody came up from behind and said, "Dave Ferris." And it was the old ra-radio operator from our crew. And this would've been--oh, it had to be around 1980. But it was a long time after was back. And he recognized me--well, I recognized him once I saw him. And we talked. And he was in Memphis, Tennessee. And then we made a trip to the Canadian Rockies, maybe eight, ten years ago. And we flew into Seattle. And the pilot was from outside of Seattle. I called and told him we were coming. So he came and met us. That's the only time I've seen him. And his wife was not well. She couldn't come with him. But we just spent an afternoon with him. And we've always exchanged Christmas cards. His wife--he was married at the time. And his wife was in contact with my mother. And my parents knew that I was alive before she knew he was alive. He was five months getting to London in the--thr-through the Underground. So she was glad to hear that I was alive, but that still didn't let her know what happened to Glen. But then, once they got back, they came through Cleveland, saw my folks, visited them and Nancy. And--but they--by then, they knew I was alive and in a prison camp. But-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So were the other members of your crew also taken prisoner?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Five of 'em.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The other five were?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Evidently, five were.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: The bombardier--the bombardier got to Paris in the Underground and disappeared. Don't know what happened. They know--they know he was alive there. And was--and might have been with the pilot. But anyhow, never got any further word on 'im. So I don't know if the landed--if the Germans got him or, or just what, but- Maybe he just decided to stay over there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: If he had, he'd of let somebody know what was going on for sure. So-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you never heard what happened to him?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I'm gonna the read the missions for the microphone here. Number--if you--if you remember anything specific about any of these, just jump in here.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: I really don't.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Number one was Frankfurt on February 4th, '44. Number two, Orleans--

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Or-Orleans was right on the--on the coast of France. You bomb submarines' pens. And that was considered a milk run because you didn't go into occupied territory, you know. Ya got--ya got antiaircraft fire, but you didn't have--didn't last very long. Ya dropped your bombs on the submarine pens and came back. So that was-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And that was on February 5th. Number three, pardon my French, Chateau D'un?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: That was another e-easy one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. On February 6th. I, I assume--wh-what--was Frankfurt the target that you really dreaded going after?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 'Cause of the--

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --flak?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: The antiaircraft fire was just horrendous all right. Now, Schweinfurt wa-was rougher because it was deeper into Germany and there was more fighter--God, we had the fighters comin' at us all the time. And you had fighters even when you went to Frankfurt, but it wasn't as far in as some of the other targets, and- So-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Missions four and five are Frankfurt on February 8 and February--maybe the 11th it looks like. Halberstadt?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: February 20th. Bramsche?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Brunswick. Wait a minute.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Osnabruck?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Osnabruck. Oh, Bramsche. I know. It was Osnabruck as I recall it. Bramsche. Bramsche. Osnabruck. And Leipzig was a deep mission and Schweinfurt.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Schweinfurt. Leipzig, eight. Schweinfurt, nine. Augsburg on the--the tenth mission on February 25th.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Pas de Calais was right on the coast of France, too. That was a short one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Watch out for the cord.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Ooo, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Trip over that. So you were not getting a whole lot of time off between missions, were you?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No. No. Well, you can see there was only a month's time between the first and last mission over there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: So I didn't have a lot of time to--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you probably weren't getting many leaves or any chances to leave the base in between.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Not a whole lot. Not a whole lot.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is this a poem you wrote?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (reading from diary) "A Toast to Heroes."

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: There's sev--there's several in there, but I don--I don't even remember the origin of 'em.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And then here--is this the last page here? No, it's not. But it says, "What a day. It won't be long now. Home in June."

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah. Sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, ya--did you do the map here of the camp?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Of the barracks?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (reading from diary) "South Compound of Stalag Luft 1." Now, this is very interesting. "An Ode to a P-38" in here.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (reading from diary) "Oh, Hedy Lamar is a beautiful gal." {laughter}

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: {laughter}

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (reading from diary) "Kriegie's Song." 'Thanks for the Memory.'" So you changed the lyrics there, huh?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (reading from diary) "Thanks for the memories of flights to Germany across the old North Sea with blazing guns." {laughter} If I could sing, I'd sing it.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: {laughter}

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (reading from diary) "Tom's Gal." Were these just things that you copied down that you heard around the camp, or...? You don't know where these came from.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Well, I don't really know. I don't really know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, this is really interesting. That's great.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: {laughter}

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {laughter} My dad had a little metal book that he wrote in during his training and combat time. But when he was captured, he was afraid to do anything, so he kept it hidden. I think he hid it in a sock or something. And so he did bring that home, and I have it. But he didn't write anything the whole time he was a prisoner.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Mmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Fortunately, when--shortly after he was liberated, he wrote down as much as he could remember. And then 40 years later, finished it.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Put it aside and then--

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: How's he doing?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He, he passed away about nin-ninteen-ninety-five.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Ah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. It, it caught up with him when he turned about 70, the malnutrition. He ended up in a labor camp. Some regular enlisted man camp and they said if you volunteered for a labor camp, you'd get more food. And he thought he'd starve. This was early '45. He thought he'd starve, so he volunteered for that. And they wen--he went to Czechoslovakia. And hard labor. {laughter} Not a lot a food and certainly not enough for the--considering the hard labor. But, I mean, he came out of it okay. He was okay until later in life. Then it caught up with him. But-

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah. It was a different ball game all right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, any other vivid memories come to mind about that time?

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Not that I think of. You know, I was tryin' to organize my thoughts. In fact--not about that time--but POWs, ex-POWs reserved a block of a hundred rooms in Washington, D.C., for, for the WWII Memorial dedication. So we got started--this was--came out, oh, a year--a year ago that they were gonna have these rooms and had a special rate and so forth. So we told our kids about it. Bingo. They all wanted to go. So we all went to Washington over Memorial Day weekend. There was 20 of us. And we got special treatment. We, we, we went by bus with motorcycle escorts, you know. {laughter} And it was a good time. And brought back a lot of memories there, too, of course, but- Well, like I said, I'm just so damn lucky to be here, and- The worst thing that's happened: We had three girls and a boy, and the son died two years ago of heart failure. And he was a fine man. {emphasis 'on fine man'} And that's the worst thing that's happened in our lives. And other than that, things have been all you could ask for, I would say.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I was in D.C., too.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: At that time?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: We didn't see each other, huh? {laughter}

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: There was a couple people there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The Library of Congress invited me to come out there because I've been doin' this.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Oh, great.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So they invited me to--I was part of the Smithsonian World War II Reunion on the Mall there--

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --where they had all those tents set up.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So yeah. We were in tents and I did interviews with veterans on this little stage in one of the tents, and then recorded one of these. Actually, we did a video oral history with a guy. And yeah. Was there for four or five days. And they paid for my room. You know, I go volunteer so I don't get any money.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Well, they should.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. They were nice. They paid a little bit for--

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: They pay your expenses for coming down here?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They paid our expenses.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And gave us some meal money and a little bit of money for doin' the interviews and paid for the room. So that was their, their reward for the volunteers.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Kinda helped them out over the past few years.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: We were gonna to go to the Smithsonian to see the airplanes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: But it turns out the airplanes are out at the airport.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {laughter} Right. Exactly. Right. __+ Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: So.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: There are some in the A-Air and Space Museum. There's some stuff in there--

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Well, the kids re--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --but the younger--the bigger ones are probably--

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: --the kids specifically wa-wanted to see a B-17--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Exactly. A. --you know. And--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: So we never--we never went to the Smithsonian.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's where we were set up: right across from the Air and Space Museum there. So yeah. My wife and son did go hang out inside there a lot and look around.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Okay

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 'Cause all the museums were open that--those four days, free. Open free.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Everything was open.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. So you could wonder into anything.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Yeah. Buses were runnin' around the Mall there. Ya get on a bus, got off anyplace you wanted to go.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: One, one of the things I got to do was I did an interview with Miss America 1944.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: {laughter}

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {laughter} Her name is Venus Ramey and she ended up--she was nose art on a B-17. They painted her picture and put her name, Venus Ramey, on the '17 that was flyin' out of Italy with the 15th Air Force. And, so yeah. We, we talked about that. {laughter}

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: {laughter}

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: __She's from Kentucky. Nice lady.

sp.speaker: David Ferris
sp.p: Oh, great. Great.
